items.prompt: In the MediatR pipeline, AuthorizationBehaviour is registered before ValidationBehaviour. What does that ordering protect?
items.answer: Anonymous callers never get validation feedback that could leak which resources exist
distractors: Validation errors get logged together with the authenticated user's name
Validators can safely assume the request's IDs already belong to the caller
Performance timing then excludes the cost of the authorization database lookups
items.explanation: The ADR calls the order load-bearing: exception logging wraps authorization, authorization precedes validation, and performance timing is innermost so it measures only the handler.

items.prompt: Why are cross-cutting concerns implemented as MediatR behaviours rather than ASP.NET Core MVC filters or middleware?
items.answer: They must also apply to non-HTTP entry points, such as tests sending through ISender
distractors: MVC filters cannot read the request body, so FluentValidation could not run there
Middleware runs after the handler has finished, which is too late to stop a bad request
Behaviours are faster because they skip model binding and the routing middleware
items.explanation: The functional test that denies an anonymous user proves authorization works with zero HTTP involved - only possible because it is a behaviour.

items.prompt: PerformanceBehaviour is the innermost behaviour. What does its 500 ms warning therefore measure?
distractors: The whole HTTP request, including model binding
Authorization plus validation, but not the handler
Only the time spent inside the EF interceptors
items.explanation: Being innermost, its stopwatch wraps only next() into the handler.

items.prompt: Which hidden cost does the behaviour pipeline add to every authenticated request?
items.answer: A database lookup of the username for log labels in two behaviours
distractors: Every request is validated twice, once on each pass through the pipeline
Each behaviour opens and commits its own DbContext transaction
The pipeline serialises requests, so only one handler can run at a time
items.explanation: The ADR lists I/O in the pipeline as a negative consequence, alongside hidden coupling.

items.prompt: A request carries [Authorize(Roles="A")] and [Authorize(Roles="B")]; the user is only in role B. What does AuthorizationBehaviour decide?
items.answer: Authorized: one flag spans all attributes, so they OR together
distractors: Forbidden: every attribute must be satisfied, as in ASP.NET Core itself
Forbidden: only the first [Authorize] attribute is ever evaluated
An exception, because two role attributes on one request are rejected at startup
items.explanation: The role loop sets authorized=true on any match across all attributes - a subtle divergence from ASP.NET Core's AND semantics.

items.prompt: Every TodoList endpoint requires authentication. What can an authenticated user still do, and why?
items.answer: Read or change other users' lists, because nothing records or checks an owner
distractors: Nothing harmful, because RequireAuthorization scopes every query to the caller
Only read other lists, because write commands are filtered by the CreatedBy column
Only see list titles, because the items are loaded through a per-user global filter
items.explanation: Authorization answers 'authenticated?' and 'in role?', never 'is this yours?'. Broken object-level authorization is OWASP API Top 10 #1.

items.prompt: A client sends colour "#BADBAD". What status does it get, and why?
items.answer: 500, because the domain exception is not mapped like validation failures
distractors: 400 ValidationProblemDetails, the same as any other invalid field
422, because the domain rejects the value after validation passes
200, because the colour is silently replaced with the default palette entry
items.explanation: Domain invariant violations and validation failures produce different contracts. The guide's preferred fix is both a validator rule and an exception mapping.

items.prompt: Which validation layer does the guide call the contract authority, and what is its weakness for cross-row rules such as a unique list title?
items.answer: FluentValidation in the pipeline; its uniqueness check races because nothing locks
distractors: Model binding; it cannot see the database, so uniqueness can never be checked there
Domain invariants; they only throw after SaveChanges has already written the row
UI hints; a maxLength attribute is trivially bypassed with curl or Postman
items.explanation: Validators aggregate every rule and can run async DB checks, but a check-then-insert across rows has no lock.

items.answer: Only when Done changes from false to true, inside the setter
distractors: Every time Done is assigned true, even if it was already true
When the handler calls Publish after SaveChanges has succeeded
Whenever any property of an already completed item is changed
items.explanation: The invariant lives in the setter, so events fire correctly from every path, including seeds and tests.

items.prompt: Domain events are published by a SaveChanges interceptor before the commit. A handler sends an email, then the save fails. What happened?
items.answer: A ghost notification: the email left even though the change never committed
distractors: Nothing: the email is queued in the same transaction and rolled back
The save is retried until it succeeds, so the email becomes true
The interceptor publishes again after the retry, sending two emails
items.explanation: Pre-commit dispatch means external side effects escape the transaction; a handler throwing would instead abort the user's save.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit the authors bought by dispatching domain events before commit?
items.answer: Handlers writing to the same DbContext commit atomically with the trigger
distractors: Events survive a process crash, because they are persisted before dispatch
Handlers run on a background thread, off the user's HTTP request
External side effects such as emails are delivered exactly once
items.explanation: No dual-write for the in-DB case. The alternative, after-commit dispatch, inverts the failure mode: save succeeds, handler fails, event lost.

items.prompt: On the synchronous SavingChanges path, the interceptor calls DispatchDomainEvents(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult(). Why is that called a landmine?
items.answer: It blocks on async work, which deadlocks wherever a synchronization context exists
distractors: It swallows every exception thrown by the domain event handlers
It dispatches each event twice, once per SaveChanges overload
It moves the save onto a new thread-pool thread, which breaks the transaction
items.explanation: Sync-over-async deadlocks when the awaited continuation needs the context the caller is blocking.

items.prompt: When should this codebase move from in-process events to a transactional outbox?
items.answer: As soon as a handler performs external I/O such as sending email
distractors: Never: in-process dispatch already guarantees at-least-once delivery
Only once an event has more than one handler registered for it
As soon as the database provider moves from SQLite to SQL Server
items.explanation: Today every handler only logs, so the ghost-notification risk is latent; the outbox is the standard answer for reliable external side effects.

items.front: Name the two authorization enforcement points in netcleanarch and what each buys.
items.back: Endpoint groups with RequireAuthorization(): fail fast with a proper HTTP 401 challenge. [Authorize] on request records enforced by AuthorizationBehaviour: works without HTTP and survives new transports. Inconsistency: only GetTodosQuery carries [Authorize].

items.front: What does a senior check, in order, to rule out IDOR in a CRUD codebase?
items.back: 1) Does the resource have an owner/tenant column? 2) Is every read filtered by it? 3) Does every write verify it before mutating? 4) Is the check centralized (global query filter / policy) or copy-pasted? 5) Do tests prove cross-user denial?

items.front: Cookie vs bearer auth: which attack each shifts onto you, and when each fits.
items.back: Cookie: HttpOnly so XSS cannot read it, but sent automatically so CSRF becomes your problem; fits an SPA served by the API. Bearer: sent explicitly so CSRF is mostly moot, but client storage makes XSS your problem; fits public APIs, cross-origin and mobile.

items.front: Why does ADR-009 call these domain events 'synchronous method calls in disguise', and what delivery guarantee do they have?
items.back: Publish awaits all handlers inline, so their latency and failures land on the user's request. Delivery is at-most-once, in-process, and lost on crash.
